### Theorem RL — zero-trace cluster exclusion

No 2-adic irreducible factor of `h` can have roots reducing to

\[
\boxed{T=0\pmod2.}
\tag{RL.2}
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\boxed{T\nmid \overline h(T)\in\mathbb F_2[T].}
\tag{RL.3}
\]

Since

\[
G_m(T):=C_m(T)+4T-6
\equiv C_m(T)
\equiv C_u(T)^r
\pmod2,
\tag{RL.4}
\]

all mod-two roots of `h` must therefore lie among the **nonzero** roots of `C_u`.

Passing to the reciprocal lift

\[
M(Z)=Z^d h(Z+Z^{-1}),
\]

which is the minimal polynomial of `z`, every mod-two root of `M` is a nontrivial odd-order root of unity of order dividing `u`.

Thus:

\[
\boxed{
\text{every mod-2 conjugate of the P1 root }z
\text{ has nontrivial odd order dividing }u.
}
\tag{RL.5}

This unifies the power-of-two case: when `u=1` there is no nontrivial odd-order residue root, so P1 is impossible. For general `u`, it removes the entire zero-trace cluster and reduces the arithmetic endpoint to the nontrivial odd divisor structure of `u`.

### Theorem FRM — full residue multiplicity

Let

\[
f(T)\in\mathbb F_2[T]
\]

be an irreducible factor occurring in the nonzero part of `G_m mod 2`, and suppose

\[
f\ne T+1.
\]

If `f` divides `h mod 2`, then in fact

\[
\boxed{f(T)^r\mid h(T)\pmod2.}
\tag{FRM.1}
\]

and the exponent is exactly `r`: if

\[
f^a\Vert h\pmod2,
\]

then

\[
\boxed{a=r.}
\tag{FRM.2}
\]

Equivalently, every nonexceptional odd-order trace orbit is binary:

```text
absent from the physical P1 factor,
or present with the full multiplicity r=2^k.
```

No partial multiplicity is possible.

The proof has two halves:

1. a local Newton polygon forces `r|a`;
2. the Littlewood reduction forces `a<=r`.

Thus the arithmetic factor problem becomes a subset-of-residue-orbits problem, apart from the single order-three trace orbit.

### Theorem NRS — non-order-three residue saturation

Let

\[
\phi(Z)\in\mathbf F_2[Z]
\]

be a monic irreducible factor of `S_u(Z)` whose roots have odd order `t>1`, with

\[
t\ne3.
\]

If

\[
\phi\mid\overline M,
\]

then in fact

\[
\boxed{\phi^r\parallel\overline M.}
\tag{NRS.1}
\]

Moreover the corresponding local factor of `M` is totally ramified of exact ramification index `r` over the unramified residue extension defined by `phi`.

Thus a hypothetical P1 factor cannot use part of a nonzero non-order-three residue cluster. It either avoids the cluster completely or consumes the entire multiplicity `r` available from the Littlewood reduction.

In particular, if

\[
3\nmid u,
\]

then there is a squarefree self-reciprocal divisor

\[
B(Z)\mid S_u(Z),
\qquad Z+1\nmid B,
\]

such that

\[
\boxed{\overline M(Z)=B(Z)^r.}

Put

\[
\delta:=2\arcsin\frac1{2D},
\qquad
q_R(D):=\frac\pi\delta,
\qquad
s:=q_R(D)-q\ge0,
\qquad
d:=d_H\in\{0,1,2\}.
\tag{UW.1}
\]

Then every directional width of the cyclic force hull satisfies the exact finite bound

\[
\boxed{
D\cos\left(\frac{(d+s+1)\delta}{2}\right)
\le
w_F(\theta)
\le D
\qquad(\theta\in\mathbb R/\pi\mathbb Z).}
\tag{UW.2}
\]

Equivalently the centered difference body obeys the concentric sandwich

\[
\boxed{
D\cos\left(\frac{(d+s+1)\delta}{2}\right)B_2
\subseteq
F-F
\subseteq
DB_2.}
\tag{UW.3}
\]

Using R2, this yields the phase-specific asymptotics

\[
\boxed{
0\le D-w_F(\theta)
\le
\frac{(d+1)^2}{8D}+o(D^{-1})
\quad\text{uniformly in }\theta.}
\tag{UW.4}
\]

Thus

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
 d_H & \displaystyle\sup_\theta(D-w_F(\theta))\\ \hline
0 & \le\dfrac1{8D}+o(D^{-1}),\\[2mm]
1 & \le\dfrac1{2D}+o(D^{-1}),\\[2mm]

\]

### Theorem PCF

Suppose `xi` is a root of unity and

\[
K_m(\xi+\xi^{-1})=0.
\]

Then

\[
\boxed{
\xi\text{ is a primitive sixth root and }m\equiv3\pmod6.
}
\tag{PCF.3}
\]

Conversely, if `m=3 mod 6`, both primitive sixth roots satisfy the equation and the corresponding trace factor is exactly

\[
\boxed{y-1.}
\tag{PCF.4}
\]

Thus `y-1` is the only trace-cyclotomic factor of `K_m`, and it occurs exactly for `m=3 mod 6`.

The physical P2 root satisfies `0<delta<pi/m`; for `m>=4`,

\[
y=2\cos\delta>2\cos(\pi/m)>1.
\]

Hence the physical root never lies in this factor. Every true P2 source must therefore use a noncyclotomic factor of `K_m`.

Write the four A/B shell-transition contacts in cyclic order as

\[
t_1,t_2,t_3,t_4,
\qquad |t_j|=1,
\]

with the D2 component-cut signs chosen so that

\[
\alpha_1L_1-\alpha_2L_2+\alpha_3L_3-\alpha_4L_4=0,
\tag{P2E.1}
\]

where `L_j=(t_j,m_j)` is the WM line/wrench vector.

In the P2 branch the two D2C switch cells pair the transitions as

\[
(t_1,t_3),
\qquad
(t_2,t_4).
\]

Then

\[
\boxed{t_3=-t_1,
\qquad
t_4=-t_2,}
\tag{P2E.2}

and each opposite pair of supporting lines is separated by

\[
\boxed{R_D:=\sqrt{D^2-1}.}

### Theorem — rotationally symmetric affine windows are not optimal when sheared

Let (S\subset\mathbb Z^2) be finite with (|S|\ge2), and suppose its difference
set (Delta=S-S) is invariant under

\[
 r(i,j)=(-j,i+j).
\]

Let (c\in(-1/2,1/2)), and let (u,v_c\in\mathbb R^2) be unit vectors with

\[
u\cdot v_c=c.
\]

Define

\[
A_c(S)=\{iu+jv_c:(i,j)\in S\},
\qquad
q_c(i,j)=i^2+j^2+2cij.
\]

Then:

1. (A_c(S)) is unit-separated. If the four basis differences occur, its
   unit-contact graph is a subgraph of the square grid and is triangle-free.
2. If (D_c=\operatorname{diam}A_c(S)) and (D_{\rm eq}) is the diameter of
   the same index set under the equilateral metric (q_{1/2}), then

### Lemma DC.1

Let `r_1,...,r_m>=0` satisfy

\[
\sum_i r_i=L,
\qquad
\sum_i(r_i-1)_+\le\nu.
\tag{2.1}
\]

If `L<=A`, then

\[
\boxed{
\sum_i r_i^3\le L^3.
}
\tag{2.2}
\]

If `L>A`, write

\[
R:=L-A,
\qquad
k:=\lfloor R\rfloor,
\qquad
\xi:=R-k\in[0,1).
\]

Then

\[
\boxed{
\sum_i r_i^3
\le
A^3+k+\xi^3.
}
\tag{2.3}
\]

Both bounds are sharp in the abstract finite optimization.

### Theorem DDM — diameter-direction measure lower semicontinuity

Let `K_j` be planar compact convex bodies with

\[
\operatorname{diam}(K_j)=1
\]

and

\[
K_j\to K
\]

in Hausdorff distance. Let `S_j` be finite sets of projective directions of unit-length chords of `K_j`. Suppose

\[
\boxed{\delta_j>0,\qquad \delta_j\to0,}
\tag{DDM.0}
\]

that distinct directions in `S_j` have projective distance at least `delta_j`, and that

\[
\liminf_j |S_j|\,\delta_j\ge c.
\]

Let `S(K)` denote the projective directions of diameter chords of `K`. Then

\[
\boxed{\mu(S(K))\ge c,}
\tag{DDM.1}
\]

where `mu` is projective-circle arc length on `R/pi Z`.

In particular, if `c>0`, the Hausdorff limit `K` cannot be a polygon.

For the HKS threshold sequence, C67 gives

\[
\delta_j=2\arcsin\frac1{2D_j}\to0,
\]

while HKN forces

\[
\frac{h_j}{D_j}\to\frac{p_c}{2}.
\]

Since `D_j delta_j->1`, DDM gives

\[
\boxed{
\mu(S(K_\infty))
\ge\frac{p_c}{2}
=1.5176561597019888\ldots .
}
\tag{DDM.2}

Sharp Hemmi equality makes `K_infty` a six-sided polygon. This gives a second contradiction for HKN.

### Theorem DPC.1 — one-pocket discrete Green-function bound

Let `P` be one OP outer pocket. Its boundary consists of

1. an old contact chain from `A` to `B` made of exactly `ell>=2` unit edges;
2. the missing force-hull side `BA`, of length `s=|A-B|`.

Then

\[
\boxed{
area(P)^2
\le
\frac{\ell^3-\ell}{6}\,(\ell-s).
}
\tag{DPC.1}
\]

Equivalently,

\[
area(P)
\le
\frac1{\sqrt6}\sqrt{\ell^3-\ell}\,\sqrt{\ell-s}.
\tag{DPC.2}
\]

This strictly improves the continuous DD bound

\[
area(P)\le\frac1{\sqrt6}\ell^{3/2}\sqrt{\ell-s}
\]

for every finite `ell`.

## Theorem

Let `za` be a source diameter edge of KKT weight

`beta=1-eta > 1/2`.

Then the positive contact graph contains a simple `z`-to-`a` path `P` with `m` unit edges such that

`m-D <= 2D eta/(1-2eta)`.

Writing

`u=(p_a-p_z)/D`

and orienting the unit edge directions of `P` from `z` to `a` as `e_1,...,e_m`, the same path satisfies

`sum_(j=1)^m |e_j-u|^2 <= 4D eta/(1-2eta)`.

Consequently, for every fixed `theta>0`, the number of path edges whose angle from `u` is at least `theta` is at most

`D eta / [(1-2eta) sin^2(theta/2)]`.

In particular, if `beta=1-o(1)` then there is a simple contact path from `z` to `a` with

`m=D+o(D)`,

`sum_j |e_j-u|^2=o(D)`,

and only `o(D)` edges outside any fixed cone about the diameter direction.

### Theorem EFAQ — fixed-angle quadrilateral under the explicit triple gap

Let `ABCD` be a convex quadrilateral of diameter at most one with

\[
AC=BD=1.
\]

Let

\[
\phi\in[2\rho,\pi/2]
\]

be the acute projective angle between the two diagonals. Assume every three of the four vertices contain a pair at distance at most `r`.

Then

\[
\boxed{
P(ABCD)
\le
\max\{\mathcal P_r(\cos(\phi/2)),\mathcal P_r(\sin(\phi/2))\},
}
\tag{EFAQ.1}

where for

\[
X\in[\sin\rho,\rho],
\qquad
Y:=\sqrt{1-X^2},
\qquad
\vartheta:=\arccos X,
\qquad
\gamma:=\arccos(r/2),
\]

we define

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal P_r(X)
:=1+r
&+\sqrt{r^2+4X^2-4rX\cos(\gamma-\vartheta)}\\
&+\sqrt{r^2+1-2r\cos(\gamma-2\vartheta)}.
\end{aligned}}
\tag{EFAQ.2}

Equivalently, with

\[
h:=\sqrt{1-r^2/4},
\]

the two residual squared side lengths are

\[
\boxed{
q_X^2
=r^2+(4-2r^2)X^2-4rhXY,
}
\tag{EFAQ.3}

\[
\boxed{
s_X^2
=1+2r^2Y^2-4rhXY,
}
\tag{EFAQ.4}

so

\[
\mathcal P_r(X)=1+r+q_X+s_X.
\]

Equality is attained in the finite quadrilateral problem: one side in the constrained opposite pair has length `r`, one adjacent side has length `1`, and the other two sides have lengths `q_X,s_X`.

For the Target C HKS angle

\[
\phi_c=p_c/2=1.5176561597019888\ldots,
\]

direct substitution gives

\[
\boxed{
P(ABCD)<3.010.

## Theorem

Work in the fully force-visible C65/C53 branch with relative-interior normalized stress `(alpha,beta)`. Let `za` be any active diameter pair, let

`b=beta_za`,

and let

`k=d_C(z,a)`

be its unweighted distance in the positive unit-contact graph.

Then

`b <= D^2/k^2`.

Equivalently,

`k <= D/sqrt(b)`.

Since every contact path consists of unit edges joining points at Euclidean distance `D`, always `k>=D`.

Thus if `b=1-eta`,

`0<=k-D <= D(1/sqrt(1-eta)-1)`

`= (eta/2+O(eta^2))D`.

In particular, C98's `b=1-o(1)` conclusion forces

### Lemma EG.2 — chord separation

Two diameter chords sharing an endpoint have projective separation at least
`2 asin(1/(2D))>=1/D`. Two disjoint diameter chords have projective separation
\[
\boxed{\phi\ge 2/D-8/D^3.}                         \tag{3.1}
\]

**Proof.** The first statement is the chord formula for two radius-`D` vectors,
using unit separation of their other endpoints. Their angle is at most `pi/3`
because the other endpoints are also at distance at most `D`.

For the second, use the actual crossing-chord coordinates
\[
A=(0,0),\quad B=(D,0),\quad C=(x,-u),\quad E=(y,v),
\]
with `u,v>0` and `0<=x<=y<=D`, relabeling and reflecting if necessary.
The projection bounds follow from membership in both radius-`D` endpoint disks.
Writing `phi` for the acute projective angle,
\[
u+v=D\sin\phi,\quad y-x=D\cos\phi,\quad
a=x+(D-y)=D(1-\cos\phi).
\]
If `phi>=2/D`, (3.1) is immediate. Otherwise
`a<=D phi^2/2<2/D<1`. Unit separation of `A,C` and `B,E` gives
\[
u\ge\sqrt{1-x^2}\ge\sqrt{1-a^2},\qquad
v\ge\sqrt{1-(D-y)^2}\ge\sqrt{1-a^2}.
\]
Consequently
\[
D\phi\ge D\sin\phi=u+v
\ge2\sqrt{1-a^2}>2\sqrt{1-4/D^2}\ge2-8/D^2.
\]

`D^-3`. For `D>=3`, its right side is at least `1/D`. ∎

```text
LEVEL I STATUS: STILL OPEN.

Favard (1929; modern statement in Campi 2005):
among convex plane bodies with given perimeter allowance and area floor,
the symmetric lens uniquely maximizes diameter. Inverted, the symmetric lens
maximizes area at fixed diameter D and perimeter P.

For P=2Dx, define alpha in [0,pi/2] by
    alpha/sin(alpha)=x.
Then
    A_lens/D^2 = L(x)
      = [alpha-sin(alpha)cos(alpha)]/[2 sin^2(alpha)].

Post-ZF has per(F)<=2h. For x=h/D<=pi/2:
    area(F)<=D^2 L(x).
OP therefore gives
    Z_ext >= n - (2/sqrt3)D^2 L(x) - h - 1.

If h/D->x:
    liminf Z_ext/D^2 >= Delta-(2/sqrt3)L(x).
Positive exactly for x<pi/2.
At tau_*=1.4781702664...:
    coefficient = 0.1071272403...
(up from 0.1038019123 under ordinary isoperimetry).

No perimeter/diameter-only argument can push the phase threshold beyond pi/2,
because the Favard extremizer becomes the disk there.
```

FAQ fixed-angle quadrilateral theorem:
Let a convex diameter-one quadrilateral have AC=BD=1 and diagonal angle

Proof: write B in the intersection of the four unit disks centered at
0,e,v,e+v. The perimeter is the convex sum of distances to those four centers,
so maximize on the boundary. On a boundary circle whose adjacent-center angle is
psi in [pi/3,2pi/3], feasibility restricts t to [psi-pi/3,pi/3]. Centering at

whose minimum on the allowed rectangle is sqrt(3)>0. Thus the maximum is an arc
endpoint, yielding the formula above. Endpoints are feasible.

### Theorem FAQ — fixed-angle small quadrilateral

Let `ABCD` be a nondegenerate convex quadrilateral of diameter at most one whose two diagonals satisfy

\[
AC=BD=1.
\]

Let

\[
\phi\in[\pi/3,2\pi/3]
\]

be the smaller oriented angle between the diagonal lines. Then

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{per}(ABCD)
\le P_4(\phi),
}
\tag{FAQ.1}

where

\[
\boxed{
P_4(\phi)
:=
2+
\sqrt{2-\sqrt3\sin\phi-\cos\phi}
+
\sqrt{2-\sqrt3\sin\phi+\cos\phi}.
}
\tag{FAQ.2}

Equality is attained. Every equality configuration has a three-vertex equilateral triangle of side one among the four quadrilateral vertices.

The function is symmetric under

\[
\phi\mapsto\pi-\phi.
\]

At `phi=pi/2`, FAQ.2 becomes

\[
2+2\sqrt{2-\sqrt3}
=2+\sqrt6-\sqrt2,
\]

recovering Tamvakis's maximal unit-diameter quadrilateral perimeter.

At the HKS angle

\[
\phi_c:=p_c/2
=1.5176561597019888\ldots,
\]

FAQ gives

\[
\boxed{
P_4(\phi_c)
=3.0349107652877701707\ldots,
}
\tag{FAQ.3}

so

\[
\boxed{
p_c-P_4(\phi_c)
=0.0004015541162074667\ldots .}
\tag{FAQ.4}

This is more than eleven times the global Tamvakis separation `p_c-P_4^*` used in TQB.

outer-to-outer stopped trains whose crosscuts lie on one complement-dual path. Assume
all train projective directions lie in an interval \(J\) of width \(W\). Fix a
diameter vertex \(v\), and let \(\mathcal L\subseteq\mathcal T\) be a subfamily such
that every train in \(\mathcal L\) is single-star two-sided braced by \(v\) in the

\[
a_D=\arcsin\frac1{2D},
\qquad
M(W,D)=2\left(\left\lfloor\frac{W}{2a_D}\right\rfloor+1\right)+1.
\tag{1}
\]

Then there is a subfamily \(\mathcal L'\subseteq\mathcal L\) and two fixed distinct
actual diameter edges
\[
